title: What helps grafted neurons survive: evidence from the team's seed papers
purpose: Survival-promoting factors for biohybrid implants like Science Corp's SU-8 microwell implant, each with its source. S01-S32 come from the team's 10 seed papers (hello_scifi/data/papers/README.md); S33-S41 come from five extra papers on the hyaluronic acid and GelMA gels the proposal now names. Companion to neuron_survival.md.

evidence_levels.seed_paper: Measured or stated in one of the 10 seed papers, and read in that paper's full text.
evidence_levels.seed_paper_protocol: A step in a seed paper's methods. The authors used it, but did not test whether it helps.
evidence_levels.cited_in_seed_paper: A seed paper describes another study. The DOI was checked against Crossref, but the original study was not read here.
evidence_levels.team_record: Taken from the team's extracted record because the full text was paywalled and not read here.
evidence_levels.outside_paper: Not one of the 10 seed papers, but read here in full text. Added on 2026-10-22 because the proposal now names HA (HyStem) and GelMA gels.
evidence_levels.outside_paper_abstract: Not a seed paper; checked from the abstract only.
evidence_levels.gap: We looked and found no direct evidence. Worth flagging as an untested region.
evidence_levels.inference: Our own suggestion that follows from the evidence, not a published result.

Lam J., Lowry W.E., Carmichael S.T. & Segura T., Delivery of iPS-NPCs to the stroke cavity within a hyaluronic acid matrix promotes the differentiation of transplanted cells, Adv. Funct. Mater. 24, 7053-7062 (2014)

notes: Quotes are not copied here. Each entry gives a location (section, figure) so a reviewer can check it against the paper.
Survival is measured differently in each paper (well occupancy, live/dead stained area, graft volume, cell counts), so numbers from different papers are not directly comparable.
Adewole et al. is cited from its peer-reviewed version (Sci. Adv. 2021). The team's records cite the 2020 bioRxiv preprint of the same study.

strategies.strategy: Put the graft on the brain surface instead of injecting it
strategies.finding: About half of the microwells still held labeled neurons three weeks after the implant was placed on the cortex. The authors say grafts in the central nervous system usually keep under 25% of their cells. They credit surface placement: it barely damages the brain's blood vessels, and they name that damage as the main cause of graft death.
strategies.numbers: 77 ± 15% of wells occupied 24 h after loading (n = 23 scaffolds); 52 ± 23% of wells with fluorescent neurons about 21 days after surgery (n = 13 implants)
strategies.setting: in vivo, mouse cortex (surface, after removing the dura)
strategies.microwell_relevance: This is the bare-well baseline the gel conditions have to beat. Science Corp's design already avoids the biggest killer, so a gel fill has to help without adding a new problem.
strategies.caveats: The two counts use different labels (DAPI vs. virus-driven fluorescence), so 52/77 is not a strict survival rate. There was no injected-graft control in the same study.

strategies.strategy: Spread the cells thinly (one cell layer)
strategies.finding: The authors suggest that a one-cell-thick graft spread evenly across the cortex avoids the harmful conditions at the center of a lump of injected cells.
strategies.microwell_relevance: A gel fill should not turn the monolayer into a thick slab. Keep the gel layer thin.
strategies.caveats: This is the authors' explanation, not a tested comparison.

strategies.strategy: Keep mechanical force on the graft low during delivery
strategies.finding: Living electrodes were left in the brain as the needle was slowly pulled back, instead of being pushed out, to keep forces on the preformed network low. The constructs survived at 1 week and 1 month.

source.location: Materials and Methods, 'Cortical implantation and intravital calcium imaging'

strategies.microwell_relevance: Brown et al. pressed the scaffold onto the brain with a stereotaxic arm. A soft gel could cushion the cells during that step (inference).
strategies.caveats: Not compared against a rougher delivery method.

strategies.strategy: Keep neurons within about 75 µm of a blood vessel
strategies.finding: Somaa et al. note that transplanted neurons are reported to survive poorly more than 75 µm from the nearest blood vessel.
strategies.numbers: 75 µm

source.location: Results, 'Cortical Progenitor Grafts Are Highly Vascularized...', paragraph 1

original.citation: Casper D. et al., Dopaminergic neurons associate with blood vessels in neural transplants, Exp. Neurol. 184, 785-793 (2003)

strategies.microwell_relevance: Science Corp's wells are 15 µm deep. A gel layer above the wells adds distance between the neurons and the host's vessels, so gel thickness should be kept well under 75 µm or the gel must let vessels in (inference).
strategies.caveats: Not read in the original; measured in dopaminergic grafts, not cortical neurons in wells.

strategies.strategy: Let host blood vessels grow into the graft
strategies.finding: Grafts were densely vascularized by vessels from the host (the vessels were not GFP-labeled, so they came from the rat). Vessels in the grafts were wider and covered less area than in normal cortex.
strategies.numbers: Vessel area: 13.9 ± 0.7% (cells + gel graft), 14.5 ± 1.5% (cells-only graft) vs 25.4 ± 0.8% (host cortex). Vessel diameter about 36 µm in grafts vs 18.6 µm in host cortex
strategies.setting: in vivo, rat cortex after stroke, 9 months

source.location: Results, 'Cortical Progenitor Grafts Are Highly Vascularized...' (Fig. 5)

strategies.microwell_relevance: Graft survival depends on host vessels reaching the cells. A gel fill should be one vessels and cells can get through (porous or degradable) (inference).
strategies.caveats: Vessel density was similar with and without the gel, so the gel's benefit here was not about vessels.

strategies.strategy: Put holes in the device so vessels can reach the cells
strategies.finding: The flexible device had circular openings so blood vessels could grow through it from the back and support the cells after implantation. The human cells survived 4 weeks and stayed attached to the device.
strategies.numbers: survival confirmed at 7 days and 4 weeks
strategies.setting: in vivo, rat forearm nerve (under the skin)
strategies.microwell_relevance: Science Corp's scaffold is bonded to a solid glass coverslip, so vessels can only come from the brain side. Any gel fill must not block that side (inference).
strategies.caveats: No with/without-holes comparison. Peripheral nerve, not brain.

strategies.strategy: Supply oxygen directly with a device
strategies.finding: The review lists electrocatalytic on-site oxygen generation and a wireless, battery-free oxygen-generating device as strategies to keep large cell-laden implants alive.
strategies.setting: cell therapies (not neural grafts in the papers read)

original.citation: Lee I. et al., Electrocatalytic on-site oxygenation for transplanted cell-based-therapies, Nat. Commun. 14, 7019 (2023)
Krishnan S.R. et al., A wireless, battery-free device enables oxygen generation and immune protection of therapeutic xenotransplants in vivo, PNAS 120, e2311707120 (2023)

strategies.microwell_relevance: A longer-term idea: electrodes already under the wells could in principle generate oxygen (inference).
strategies.caveats: Not read in the originals; not shown for neurons in these papers.

strategies.strategy: Inject cells in a laminin-mimicking peptide gel (IKVAV)
strategies.finding: A self-assembling peptide gel carrying IKVAV, a short piece of laminin that neurons stick to, made human cortical grafts about 3 times larger, with about 3.6 times as many cells and a higher share of neurons, than cells injected alone. Every recorded neuron in the gel grafts received both excitatory and inhibitory inputs. The gel alone, without cells, gave little protection.
strategies.numbers: At 36 weeks: graft volume 10.7 ± 3.8 vs 3.5 ± 1.8 mm³; cells 30.5 × 10⁵ vs 8.5 × 10⁵; neurons 69.6 ± 2.9% vs 49.7 ± 8.8% of graft cells; all recorded gel-graft neurons had both excitatory and inhibitory inputs, vs 4/5 (excitatory) and 3/5 (inhibitory) in cells-only grafts
strategies.setting: in vivo, stroke cavity in rat sensorimotor cortex, 9 months
strategies.cells: human ESC-derived cortical progenitors (in immunodeficient rats)

source.location: Results, 'SAP Scaffolds Provide Structural and Biochemical Support...' (Fig. 3) and 'Human ESC-Derived Neurons...' (Fig. 6)

strategies.recipe: Fmoc-DDIKVAV peptide dissolved at 20 mg/mL, pH adjusted to 7.4, sheared and mixed 1:1 with cells (final 10 mg/mL gel, 50,000 cells/µL). Stiffness similar to rat brain (Fig. 1I). Gel fibers still visible at 9 months.
strategies.microwell_relevance: A strong candidate for the non-conductive gel condition: soft like brain, gels at body pH, carries a laminin cue, and lasted 9 months in vivo (inference).
strategies.caveats: Injected into a stroke cavity, not loaded into microwells. Human cells in immunodeficient rats.

strategies.strategy: Grow neurons as 3D aggregates inside a hydrogel tube with a collagen–laminin core
strategies.finding: Between day 10 and day 28 in culture, neurons in hydrogel microcolumns lost much less viability than neurons grown flat on plastic (2.4 to 3 times less). They survived at least 40 days in vitro.
strategies.numbers: Viability at 10 → 28 days in vitro: unidirectional 80.3% → 68.1% (15.2% drop); bidirectional 84.8% → 69.0% (18.6% drop); flat culture 97.7% → 53.6% (45% drop)

source.location: Results, 'μTENN viability' (fig. S1, G and H); Discussion, paragraph 4

strategies.recipe: 3% agarose microcolumns (398 µm outer / 180 µm inner diameter) filled with 1 mg/mL collagen + 1 mg/mL laminin; aggregates made by spinning neurons into pyramidal PDMS wells (200g, 5 min); Neurobasal + B27 + GlutaMAX.
strategies.microwell_relevance: Supports the idea that a soft 3D, ECM-filled environment slows neuron loss over weeks compared with a flat stiff surface. A bare SU-8 well is closer to the flat case (inference).
strategies.caveats: Flat cultures started higher at day 10 (97.7%), so the benefit is a slower decline, not better early survival. Aggregates of thousands of neurons differ from Science Corp's one neuron per well.

strategies.strategy: Hydrogel-encased neurons survive in the brain with a mild glial reaction
strategies.finding: Living electrodes (neuron aggregates inside agarose microcolumns) survived and kept their structure at 1 week and 1 month in rat cortex, were active on calcium imaging at 5 and 10 days, and caused only a modest glial and microglial reaction.
strategies.numbers: survival at 1 week and 1 month (histology); activity at 5 and 10 days

source.location: Results, 'Implantation and intravital calcium imaging' (Figs. 5 and 6)

strategies.microwell_relevance: Shows a hydrogel housing can protect neurons in vivo for at least a month, longer than the proposal's 21-day window.
strategies.caveats: Survival was shown qualitatively (no percentage reported in vivo).

strategies.strategy: Use a gelatin-containing gel as the cell layer
strategies.finding: Astrocytes grown inside a PVA–gelatin gel on top of a conductive PEDOT gel electrode reached 1.5 times the cell density of the same gel on glass. Metabolic activity rose about 41% from day 3 to day 14 in both. Medium soaked with the coating was not toxic to Schwann cells. Gelatin gives cells sites to grip (integrin binding) and sites they can digest, so they can remodel the gel.
strategies.numbers: 55,000 vs 35,000 astrocytes per cm² at 14 days; spreading 1800 vs 1400 µm² per cell; +41% metabolic activity day 3 → 14; Schwann cell density +23.1% vs plastic in conditioned medium
strategies.cells: rat hippocampal astrocytes; Schwann cell line
strategies.recipe: PVA-norbornene and gelatin-norbornene at 25:75 by weight, 10% w/v in DPBS, dithiothreitol crosslinker, eosin Y, visible light (555 nm, 15 mW/cm², 3 min); astrocytes at 5 × 10⁶ cells/mL.
strategies.microwell_relevance: A ready recipe for a cell-friendly top layer over a conductive gel in the 'conductive gel' condition (inference).
strategies.caveats: Astrocytes and Schwann cells, not neurons; in vitro only. The authors note cells may have settled toward the stiffer bottom layer.

strategies.strategy: Hold cells on the device with a fibrin gel
strategies.finding: Human cells seeded on a fibrin hydrogel layer on the electrode array survived 4 weeks in vivo and stayed closely attached to the device.
strategies.numbers: fibrinogen 3.125-25 mg/mL, thrombin 1 U/mL, CaCl₂ 20 mM (final)
strategies.setting: in vivo, rat (under the skin, next to the forearm nerve)
strategies.microwell_relevance: Fibrin is a candidate gel, but see S13 and S14: it breaks down within about a week, so it would mostly act during the first days (inference).
strategies.caveats: Muscle cells, not neurons.

strategies.strategy: A thin fibrin coating that dissolves within a week
strategies.finding: Microelectrodes seeded with hippocampal neurons or astrocytes and covered by a thin biodegradable fibrin coating reduced reactive astrocytes without changing electrode impedance. The fibrin was fully reabsorbed within 7 days, which may avoid the gel swelling and pushing cells away from the electrodes.
strategies.numbers: reabsorbed within 7 days

source.location: 'Cell-seeded electrodes to improve the device-tissue interface', paragraph 3

original.citation: De Faveri S. et al., Bio-inspired hybrid microelectrodes: a hybrid solution to improve long-term performance of chronic intracortical implants, Front. Neuroeng. 7, 7 (2014)

strategies.microwell_relevance: Shows a temporary gel can help through the risky first days without the long-term swelling problem (inference).
strategies.caveats: Not read in the original.

strategies.strategy: Make sure the gel lasts as long as the cells need it
strategies.finding: Neural stem cells held in an alginate gel inside a hollow well on a probe supported nearby host neurons for 1 month, mainly through the protective factors they released. Later, the gel broke down and neuron viability near the implant fell. Separately, PVA–gelatin gels can lose up to 30% of their weight in 28 days in buffer.
strategies.numbers: 1 month benefit, then decline; PVA–gelatin up to 30% weight loss in 28 days

source.location: 'Cell-seeded electrodes to improve the device-tissue interface', paragraph 1

original.citation: Purcell E.K. et al., In vivo evaluation of a neural stem cell-seeded prosthesis, J. Neural Eng. 6, 026005 (2009)

also_see.location: Section 3.4, paragraph 3 (PVA–gelatin weight loss, citing earlier studies)

strategies.microwell_relevance: The proposal runs to day 21, so measure gel thickness or mass at days 1, 7 and 21 alongside survival (the proposal already flags gel degradation as a risk).
strategies.caveats: Not read in the original.

strategies.strategy: Do not polymerize a conductive polymer around living neurons
strategies.finding: When PEDOT was polymerized directly around living neural cells, they stayed viable for almost a week and then died by apoptosis (programmed cell death). The review suggests the polymer disrupted their adhesion signals and caused oxidative stress.
strategies.numbers: viability kept about 1 week, then apoptosis

source.location: 'Cell-seeded electrodes to improve the device-tissue interface', paragraph 2

original.citation: Richardson-Burns S.M. et al., Polymerization of the conducting polymer poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT) around living neural cells, Biomaterials 28, 1539-1552 (2007)

strategies.microwell_relevance: In the conductive-gel condition, make and rinse the conductive gel before the neurons go in, and keep neurons in a cell-friendly layer (inference).
strategies.caveats: Not read in the original.

strategies.strategy: Layered design: conductive gel underneath, cell-friendly biodegradable gel on top
strategies.finding: Layered devices with a cell-laden biodegradable gel on top of a conductive gel addressed the viability loss of the neural progenitor cells inside, and the conductive layer improved charge storage and injection over bare platinum. However, neurites grew little and no synapses formed.

source.location: 'Cell-seeded electrodes to improve the device-tissue interface', paragraph 3

original.citation: Goding J. et al., A living electrode construct for incorporation of cells into bionic devices, MRS Commun. 7, 487-495 (2017)

also_see.location: the same group's newer version of this design (S11)

strategies.microwell_relevance: Suggests the conductive-gel condition be built as two layers. The poor outgrowth warns that a gel fill could trap neurites, which is why the proposal measures neurites crossing the well rim.
strategies.caveats: Not read in the original.

strategies.strategy: Neutralize PEDOT:PSS before adding cells
strategies.finding: PEDOT:PSS solutions and pure PEDOT:PSS gels in water are strongly acidic (pH 1-2) because of the PSS. Soaking in phosphate-buffered saline neutralizes them.
strategies.numbers: pH 1-2 in deionized water

source.location: Results, 'Electrical conductivity of pure PEDOT:PSS hydrogels', paragraph 2

strategies.microwell_relevance: Equilibrate any PEDOT:PSS gel in buffer, then in culture medium, and check the pH before loading neurons (inference; the paper did no cell work).
strategies.caveats: The survival link is our inference.

strategies.strategy: Prefer pure, stable conductive gels without nano-fillers, but expect them to be stiffer than brain
strategies.finding: Pure PEDOT:PSS hydrogels (80-87% water) were stable for 3 months in buffer. The authors note that nano-filler additives can make gels uneven, unstable and potentially toxic to cells. These gels are still 2-10 MPa, far stiffer than brain (about 1-30 kPa per the Boufidis review).
strategies.numbers: Young's modulus 2-10 MPa in PBS; stable 3 months; water 80-87 wt%

source.location: Introduction, paragraph 3; Results, 'Mechanical stability' and 'Mechanical properties'

strategies.microwell_relevance: Shows the trade-off the team's maps show: the most conductive gels are not brain-soft. Separating stiffness from conductivity, as the proposal plans, matters.
strategies.caveats: No cell or survival data in this paper.

strategies.strategy: Use soft materials to reduce scarring and neuron loss around the implant
strategies.finding: The review reports that soft hydrogel coatings such as PEG and PVA reduce glial scarring and neuronal loss around rigid electrodes, and that PEG-DMA coatings reduce scarring caused by micromotion. Liu et al. built conductive hydrogel electronics with kilopascal stiffness. The team's record says inflammation at 6 weeks was similar to a sham surgery.

original.citation: Spencer K.C. et al., Characterization of mechanically matched hydrogel coatings to improve the biocompatibility of neural implants, Sci. Rep. 7, 1952 (2017)

also_see.location: team record liu-2019-pedot-pss-electrically-c-3bf2c3 (notes); full text not read here

strategies.microwell_relevance: Supports filling rigid SU-8 (about 2 GPa) with a soft gel, mainly to protect host tissue and the interface.
strategies.caveats: About host tissue, not grafted cells. Liu 2019 detail is from the team record, not checked here.

strategies.strategy: Coat the wells with poly-D-lysine and laminin
strategies.finding: Science Corp coated the SU-8 microwells with poly-D-lysine (0.1 mg/mL) and laminin (0.1 mg/mL) for at least an hour before loading neurons.
strategies.numbers: 0.1 mg/mL each, at least 1 h
strategies.setting: in vitro loading, then in vivo
strategies.microwell_relevance: The proposal keeps this coating the same in every condition, which is right: it makes the gel the only difference.
strategies.caveats: Not compared with other coatings.

strategies.strategy: Adhesion-protein coatings (laminin, L1) on implants
strategies.finding: The review reports that a laminin coating on silicon arrays briefly increased microglia but reduced the glial scar at 1 month, and that an L1 (neural cell adhesion molecule) coating increased nearby neuron density and reduced microglial activation over 16 weeks.
strategies.numbers: 1 month (laminin); 16 weeks (L1)
strategies.setting: in vivo, rat and mouse cortex

original.citation: He W., McConnell G.C. & Bellamkonda R.V., Nanoscale laminin coating modulates cortical scarring response around implanted silicon microelectrode arrays, J. Neural Eng. 3, 316-326 (2006)
Golabchi A. et al., Neuroadhesive protein coating improves the chronic performance of neuroelectronics in mouse brain, Biosens. Bioelectron. 155, 112096 (2020)

strategies.microwell_relevance: Possible future condition: an L1 coating on the well walls, tested against the standard PDL + laminin (inference).
strategies.caveats: About host neurons near implants, not grafted neurons. Not read in the originals.

strategies.strategy: Post-treat SU-8 to make it less toxic
strategies.finding: After patterning the SU-8 wells, Science Corp gave them an extra UV flood exposure (about 1.86 J), which they say was to improve biocompatibility, followed by a hard bake up to 200 °C.
strategies.numbers: about 1.86 J UV flood; hard bake 95 °C 5 min, then 200 °C 2 min

original.citation: Nemani K.V. et al., In vitro and in vivo evaluation of SU-8 biocompatibility, Mater. Sci. Eng. C 33, 4453-4459 (2013)

strategies.microwell_relevance: Use the identical SU-8 processing for bare and gel-filled wells, so leftover chemicals from the resist can't explain any difference (inference).
strategies.caveats: Brown et al. cite Nemani 2013 for this step; we did not read Nemani 2013.

strategies.strategy: Use embryonic neurons from a genetically matched donor
strategies.finding: Science Corp used embryonic cortical neurons from the same mouse strain as the hosts, so no immune-suppressing drugs were needed. Neurons this young are mostly excitatory, and no tumors or overgrowth were seen. The authors say this donor choice may be a key reason for the high survival, and that it is not an option for human patients.
strategies.numbers: embryonic day E14.5-E15.5 (Methods says E14.5-E16.5); C57BL/6J into C57BL/6J
strategies.microwell_relevance: Keep the cell source fixed across conditions (as the proposal says). For humans, an iPSC source plus an immune strategy (S27-S30) would be needed.
strategies.caveats: The authors' judgement, not a tested comparison.

strategies.strategy: Prepare and load cells gently
strategies.finding: Science Corp dissected cortex into ice-cold medium containing 15 mM kynurenic acid, dissociated it with papain, and washed it through trypsin inhibitor. Cells were kept in Neurobasal medium with B27 and GlutaMAX, spun into the wells (300 g, 5 min), and given 2 hours and then an overnight rest in the incubator before surgery.
strategies.numbers: 1 × 10⁶ neurons/mL; 300 RCF for 5 min; 2 h + overnight recovery
strategies.microwell_relevance: Copy this protocol exactly for every condition. Our note: kynurenic acid blocks glutamate receptors and is commonly added to protect neurons from excitotoxic damage during dissection; the paper doesn't say why it was used.
strategies.caveats: A protocol, not a tested comparison.

strategies.strategy: Keep the cell-loaded device sterile instead of re-sterilizing it
strategies.finding: Rochford et al. kept the cell-loaded devices sterile through culture and did not sterilize them again before implanting; control devices without cells were sterilized in 70% ethanol. Boulingre et al. autoclaved the conductive gel layer before adding the cell-containing layer.
strategies.microwell_relevance: Sterilize the SU-8 and any gel before loading neurons. Once cells are in, sterile handling is the only option, because ethanol or heat would kill them (inference).
strategies.caveats: Practical handling, not a survival measurement.

strategies.strategy: Protect the graft during the first few days
strategies.finding: Brown et al. write that grafted neurons die mainly by apoptosis in the first few days after transplant, driven by low oxygen and immune attack after the blood-brain barrier is damaged.

source.location: Discussion, paragraph 2 (timing cited to refs 18 and 52; low survival after microinjection to refs 18-21, 51, 52)

original.citation: Emgård M. et al., Patterns of cell death and dopaminergic neuron survival in intrastriatal nigral grafts, Exp. Neurol. 160, 279-288 (1999) (ref. 52)
Sortwell C.E., Pitzer M.R. & Collier T.J., Time course of apoptotic cell death within mesencephalic cell suspension grafts, Exp. Neurol. 165, 268-277 (2000) (ref. 51)

strategies.microwell_relevance: The proposal's day-1 and day-7 survival counts will catch this early window. Protective steps (anti-inflammatories, temporary gels) matter most in week 1 (inference).
strategies.caveats: The cited studies are on dopaminergic grafts; not read in the originals.

strategies.strategy: Give an anti-inflammatory drug (dexamethasone)
strategies.finding: Science Corp gave mice dexamethasone (2 mg/kg) as an anti-inflammatory at each surgery. The review reports that dexamethasone-coated probes reduced inflammation and neuron loss around implants, and that dexamethasone can be released from electrodes on demand.
strategies.numbers: 2 mg/kg at surgery

original.citation: Zhong Y. & Bellamkonda R.V., Dexamethasone-coated neural probes elicit attenuated inflammatory response and neuronal loss compared to uncoated neural probes, Brain Res. 1148, 15-27 (2007)
Boehler C. et al., Actively controlled release of Dexamethasone from neural microelectrodes in a chronic in vivo study, Biomaterials 129, 176-187 (2017)

strategies.microwell_relevance: A gel fill could carry dexamethasone and release it locally during the first week (inference).
strategies.caveats: Brown et al. did not test with vs without dexamethasone.

strategies.strategy: Use immunodeficient hosts (stand-in for immunosuppression) when grafting human cells
strategies.finding: Rochford et al. and Somaa et al. implanted human cells into athymic nude rats, which lack T cells, to help the human cells survive. Rochford et al. describe this as standing in for immune-suppressing drugs in human patients. Somaa et al. note these rats are prone to infections over long studies.

also_see.location: Experimental Procedures; Results, 'Cortical Progenitor Grafts Are Highly Vascularized...', paragraph 3

strategies.microwell_relevance: Only matters if the team's experiment uses human cells in vivo; the proposal is in vitro first.
strategies.caveats: No with/without comparison.

strategies.strategy: Block TNF-α signaling (with cell sorting) after grafting
strategies.finding: A CRISPR screen found that p53-driven cell death, switched on by TNF-α–NF-κB signaling, limits the survival of grafted stem-cell-derived dopamine neurons. Sorting the cells and treating with adalimumab, an approved TNF-α blocker, enabled efficient engraftment in a Parkinson's mouse model.

original.citation: Kim T.W. et al., TNF-NF-κB-p53 axis restricts in vivo survival of hPSC-derived dopamine neurons, Cell 187, 3671-3689.e23 (2024)

strategies.microwell_relevance: A drug-based survival booster that could be tested on top of the best gel later (inference).
strategies.caveats: Checked from the abstract and summaries only, not the full text.

strategies.strategy: Co-transplant regulatory T cells with the neurons
strategies.finding: Fewer than 10% of grafted dopamine neurons survived at 2 weeks, mostly because of inflammation from needle trauma. Adding the animal's own regulatory T cells (immune cells that calm inflammation) to the graft suppressed that inflammation, protected the neurons and improved outcomes in rodent Parkinson's models.
strategies.numbers: under 10% survival at 2 weeks without Tregs

original.citation: Park T.-Y. et al., Co-transplantation of autologous Treg cells in a cell therapy for Parkinson's disease, Nature 619, 606-615 (2023)

strategies.microwell_relevance: Injection-specific; surface microwells avoid most needle trauma (S01), but this shows how much inflammation alone can kill.
strategies.caveats: Checked from the abstract and summaries only, not the full text.

strategies.strategy: Add support cells (stem cells or astrocytes) that release protective factors
strategies.finding: The review reports that neural stem cells in a probe-mounted gel protected nearby host neurons for a month, mainly through factors they secreted, and that neural progenitors on laminin-coated silicon probes reduced glial scarring, with astrocytes around the implant releasing neurotrophic (neuron-supporting) factors for up to a week. It calls including glial cells 'often overlooked'.

source.location: 'Cell-seeded electrodes to improve the device-tissue interface', paragraph 1; 'Challenges and outlook' (biohybrid), paragraph 1

original.citation: Purcell E.K. et al., In vivo evaluation of a neural stem cell-seeded prosthesis, J. Neural Eng. 6, 026005 (2009)
Azemi E., Gobbel G.T. & Cui X.T., Seeding neural progenitor cells on silicon-based neural probes, J. Neurosurg. 113, 673-681 (2010)

strategies.microwell_relevance: A later experiment could co-load astrocytes with neurons, which Boulingre's gel already supports (S11). Keep it separate from the first bare-vs-gel test so only one thing changes (inference).
strategies.caveats: Not read in the originals.

strategies.strategy: Release growth factors from the gel
strategies.finding: The review reports that hydrogels containing adhesion molecules or ECM proteins can also deliver nerve growth factors and anti-inflammatory drugs (dexamethasone, α-MSH), for example neurotrophin-eluting hydrogel coatings on stimulating electrodes. It also notes that in the early 'cone electrode', replacing a living nerve fragment with growth factors gave less neurite ingrowth.

original.citation: Winter J.O., Cogan S.F. & Rizzo J.F. III, Neurotrophin-eluting hydrogel coatings for neural stimulating electrodes, J. Biomed. Mater. Res. B 81B, 551-563 (2007)
Kennedy P.R., The cone electrode: a long-term electrode that records from neurites grown onto its recording surface, J. Neurosci. Methods 29, 181-193 (1989)

strategies.microwell_relevance: A gel fill can double as a drug or growth-factor reservoir. That adds a variable, so it fits a follow-up, not the first comparison (inference).
strategies.caveats: Not read in the originals. The cone-electrode point is about neurite ingrowth, not survival.

strategies.category: Candidate gels in the current proposal
strategies.strategy: Deliver cells in a HyStem-HP hyaluronic acid–heparin–gelatin gel
strategies.finding: Neural progenitor cells injected into the brain inside HyStem-HP gel survived twice as well at 2 weeks as cells injected without it, in mice with normal immune systems and no immune-suppressing drugs. The gel formed a zone around the graft that kept microglia (the brain's immune cells) out. The paper describes the gel as transparent, setting over about 30 minutes.
strategies.numbers: About 8,000 vs 4,000 surviving cells out of 100,000 injected (P = .035, n = 6 per group). Embryonic-stem-cell-derived progenitors also doubled, though under 1% survived either way (the text gives 0.3% and 0.6% in an order that looks swapped).
strategies.setting: in vivo, mouse stroke cavity, 2 weeks; plus in vitro
strategies.cells: mouse embryonic cortex progenitors; mouse ES-derived progenitors

source.location: Methods, 'Hyaluronan-Heparin-Collagen Hydrogel'; Results, first and second sections (Figs. 1, 3)

strategies.recipe: HyStem-HP (Glycosan): thiol-modified hyaluronan + heparin sulfate + gelatin, crosslinked with PEG diacrylate. 100,000 cells in 1 µL + 4 µL HA/heparin + 1 µL gelatin + 1 µL crosslinker; injected while liquid.
strategies.microwell_relevance: Direct support for the proposal's HyStem choice: the same product family, in the brain, with a measured survival gain and a clear gel.
strategies.caveats: Progenitor cells injected into a stroke cavity, not neurons in microwells. HyStem-HP includes heparin; plain HyStem kits may behave differently.

strategies.category: Candidate gels in the current proposal
strategies.strategy: Expect the gel's benefit to show mostly when there is an immune or stress challenge
strategies.finding: In immune-deficient (NSG) mice, HA gels did not raise graft survival. Lam et al. found 38,000 vs 30,000 surviving cells at 1 week, not significant, and Moshayedi et al. saw equal survival. In normal mice given tacrolimus (an immune-suppressing drug), Moshayedi's optimized HA gel did raise 2-week survival, and cells injected without gel survived in very low numbers. In culture, HyStem-HP helped only modestly with full nutrients and growth factors, but substantially when they were withdrawn.
strategies.numbers: Lam: 38,000 (gel) vs 30,000 (no gel) of 100,000 at 1 week, P > 0.05. Zhong: in vitro survival gain modest with support, large under nutrient and growth-factor withdrawal (P = .007 and .002).
strategies.setting: in vivo, mouse stroke; in vitro
strategies.cells: human iPSC-derived and mouse neural progenitors

also_see.location: Section 3.7 'Effects of HA gels on cell survival in vivo' (Fig. 3C)
Results, 'Hydrogel Supports the Survival of NPCs Deprived of Growth Factors in Culture' (Fig. 5)

strategies.microwell_relevance: The proposal's in vitro bare-vs-gel test may show little difference in rich medium even if the gel helps in the brain. Adding a stress condition, such as a short growth-factor or B27 withdrawal, could reveal a protective effect (inference).
strategies.caveats: Progenitors, not mature neurons; stroke injection model.

strategies.category: Candidate gels in the current proposal
strategies.strategy: Make the gel about as soft as brain (around 300 Pa)
strategies.finding: Brain-soft HA gels (storage modulus about 300 Pa) caused no more inflammation than buffer, while a stiffer version (above 1,000 Pa) raised reactive astrocytes in healthy brain and microglia in stroke brain. Making the crosslinker degradable or not did not change inflammation. In the stroke cavity, a 350 Pa gel filled the space best.
strategies.numbers: about 300 Pa (soft) vs over 1,000 Pa (stiff), measured as storage modulus G' by shear rheology
strategies.setting: in vivo, mouse striatum and stroke cavity, 2 weeks

source.location: Sections 2.1 'Hydrogel Design' and 2.2 'Inflammatory Response to Hydrogel' (Fig. 2)

strategies.microwell_relevance: The proposal's stiffness range (0.5-50 kPa) starts above these brain-soft gels. HyStem kits reach about 23-3,500 Pa G' (team reference 'hystem'), so a level near 300 Pa is possible. Note that G' is not Young's modulus, as the proposal already warns (inference).
strategies.caveats: Gel injected into tissue, not filling 15 µm wells.

strategies.category: Candidate gels in the current proposal
strategies.strategy: Use crosslinks that the cells' own enzymes can cut, so vessels can grow in
strategies.finding: HA gels crosslinked with a peptide that MMPs (enzymes released by cells and injured tissue) can cut had far more blood vessels growing in at 2 weeks than the same gel with an uncuttable crosslinker, which had very few. Vessels were found inside the gel as early as 2 weeks. Gels loaded with more cells broke down faster: 100,000 cells lost a lot of gel volume between weeks 2 and 6, while 50,000 cells left it mostly intact for 6 weeks.
strategies.numbers: Vessel ingrowth significantly higher with the MMP-cleavable crosslinker (Fig. 1Bviii); gel volume loss depended on cell number (Fig. 2)
strategies.setting: in vivo, mouse stroke cavity, 2-9 weeks

source.location: Sections 3.2 'Crosslinker sensitivity to MMPs in vivo' and 3.5 'HA gel degradation and angiogenesis'

strategies.microwell_relevance: Fits the proposal's 'protease-sensitive linkers' for setting degradation time, and adds a reason: cleavable gels let vessels in (see S04, S05). Cell density will also shift degradation time, so measure gel loss at the actual loading density (inference).
strategies.caveats: Stroke cavity, not microwells.

strategies.category: Candidate gels in the current proposal
strategies.strategy: Rely on the gel to calm the immune response around the graft
strategies.finding: HA gels reduced microglia and macrophages in and around grafts in two studies. In Zhong et al. the gel formed a zone microglia seemed unable to enter, with fewer Iba1-positive cells in the graft (31 ± 7 vs 19 ± 4 per mm³). Lam et al. saw a lower Iba1 signal with the gel. Zhong et al. propose this is a main reason the gel improved survival.
strategies.numbers: Iba1+ cells 31 ± 7/mm³ (no gel) vs 19 ± 4/mm³ (gel), P = .003 (ES-derived progenitors)

source.location: Results, 'Hydrogel Diminishes the Infiltration of Microglia/Macrophage Cells Into the Graft' and the ES-NPC section (Figs. 3, 4)

strategies.microwell_relevance: Brown et al. name immune attack in the first days as a main cause of graft death (S26), so a gel that shields cells from microglia during that window is exactly the proposal's 'temporary protection' idea (inference).
strategies.caveats: Mechanism is the authors' interpretation.

strategies.category: Candidate gels in the current proposal
strategies.strategy: A viscous gel protects cells pushed through a thin needle
strategies.finding: Injecting at high cell density or through a fine 33-gauge needle lowered viability more for cells in buffer than for cells in HA gel; the gel's advantage was significant at 90,000 cells/µL. Injection speed (0.3-0.9 µL/min) made no difference either way.
strategies.numbers: Gel improved viability at 90,000 cells/µL (P < 0.05); no effect of infusion speed 0.3-0.9 µL/min
strategies.microwell_relevance: Science Corp loads wells by centrifugation, not needles, so this matters only if the team ever injects cells. Mixing cells into gel before spinning them into wells would be a different stress worth checking (inference).
strategies.caveats: In vitro; not about microwells.

strategies.category: Candidate gels in the current proposal
strategies.strategy: Mature neurons inside an HA gel (with RGD and heparin) and transplant them in it
strategies.finding: About 5 times more dopamine neurons survived when they were matured inside a stiffness-tuned HA gel carrying RGD (a cell-grip peptide) and heparin and transplanted in it, compared with neurons scraped off ordinary 2D plates. The paper notes only 1-5% of such neurons usually survive.
strategies.numbers: about 5× more surviving neurons
strategies.microwell_relevance: Suggests letting neurons settle inside the gel in the well before implanting, rather than adding gel at the last minute (inference).
strategies.caveats: Abstract only; injected grafts, not microwells.

strategies.strategy: Transplant less mature cells
strategies.finding: Immature cortical progenitors survived the transplant process with the least cell death, while more mature neurons had the most acute death. The dying mature cells harmed the host tissue and cancelled out the benefits of the hydrogel vehicle, which on its own gave some benefit.
strategies.cells: human cortically specified neuroepithelial progenitors at different maturities
strategies.microwell_relevance: Science Corp loads young embryonic neurons (S23). If the team uses iPSC-derived cells, record their maturity at loading, because it may matter as much as the gel (inference).
strategies.caveats: Abstract only; hyaluronan/methylcellulose gel, not HyStem or GelMA.

strategies.category: Candidate gels in the current proposal
strategies.strategy: GelMA: no direct neuron-survival evidence found
strategies.finding: We did not find a study measuring primary neuron survival inside GelMA. The closest is the team's existing reference (Wu et al. 2019): PC12 cells grown on GelMA surfaces of different stiffness, which affected viability and neurite length. GelMA is set with a photoinitiator and light, which is an extra stress on cells not present with HyStem's chemical crosslinking.

original.citation: Wu Y. et al., The influence of the stiffness of GelMA substrate on the outgrowth of PC12 cells, Biosci. Rep. 39, BSR20181748 (2019)

strategies.microwell_relevance: If GelMA is used, record photoinitiator type and concentration, light wavelength, intensity and time, and include a light-only control without gel. This is a real gap the experiment would fill (inference).
strategies.caveats: A limited search, not a systematic review.

takeaways_checked_against: hello_scifi/docs/proposal.md on origin/main at commit 130d5c7 (clear, degradable, non-conductive gel first; conductive gel as a follow-up)
takeaways_for_the_microwell_experiment: Most graft death happens in the first few days, from low oxygen and inflammation (S01, S26). That supports the proposal's idea of a temporary gel that protects cells early and then gets out of the way.

The best direct evidence for the proposal's gel choice: HyStem-HP, a clear HA–heparin–gelatin gel, doubled graft survival in the brain at 2 weeks and kept microglia out of the graft (S33, S37). A tuned HA gel gave about 5 times more surviving neurons (S39).

The gel's benefit may only show under stress. HA gels made no difference in immune-deficient mice but helped in mice with an immune response, and in culture HyStem-HP helped most when growth factors were withdrawn. An in vitro test in rich medium could miss the effect, so consider adding a stress condition (S34).

Go soft: brain-like gels near 300 Pa caused no more inflammation than buffer, while gels above 1 kPa raised glial and microglial reactions (S35). The proposal's 0.5-50 kPa range could add a level near 300 Pa.

Use crosslinks that the cells' enzymes (MMPs) can cut: they let blood vessels into the gel within 2 weeks. More cells break the gel down faster, so measure degradation at the real loading density (S36, S04, S05).
Keep the gel layer thin above the 15 µm wells, ideally well under 75 µm, so it doesn't become an oxygen barrier (S02, S04).
Laminin cues help: an IKVAV peptide gel tripled graft size (S08), and collagen–laminin 3D environments slowed neuron loss over weeks (S09, S10).
GelMA has no direct neuron-survival data that we found, and it adds a light-curing step. If it is used, record the photoinitiator and light dose and include a light-only control (S41).
Keep everything else identical across conditions: SU-8 processing, PDL + laminin coating, cell source, cell maturity and loading protocol (S20, S22, S23, S24, S40).
For the conductive-gel follow-up: make the conductive gel before the cells go in, neutralize it, and put cells in a separate cell-friendly top layer (S11, S15, S16, S17).
Later ideas: dexamethasone released from the gel, co-loaded astrocytes, L1 coatings, TNF-α blockade (S21, S27, S29, S31).
